title: B+trees
goal: By the end you can explain why a database index is a short, wide tree of pages, trace an insert that splits a leaf and grows a new root, read PostgreSQL's B-tree pages with pageinspect, say how a copy-on-write B-tree such as LMDB's avoids overwriting pages, and build an order-4 B+tree with range scans.

warmup.q: A PostgreSQL table holds 1,000,000 payments with a B-tree primary key on `id`. How many index pages does `WHERE id = 424242` read?
options: About 20, one per level of a balanced binary tree
1, because the index maps each key straight to its row
All 2,745 pages of the index, but they are small
warmup.why: Each index page holds a few hundred keys, so three levels cover a million rows, and a lookup reads one page per level. The first Try it shows `Buffers: shared hit=4`: three index pages and the heap page with the row. Twenty is what a tree with one key per node would need. A hash index could jump nearly straight to a key, but a B-tree walks down from the root.

sections.h: Finding one row needs a sorted structure that is short and wide
sections.body:
Lessons 2 and 3 gave the engine pages and a cache for them, but no quick way to find one row. Try payment 424242 in a table of a million rows. The table is a heap (lesson 2 of this track), so rows sit wherever there was room, in no order. The only way to find one row is to read every page: 6,400 pages of 8 KB, about 24 ms in the first Try it. A payment API that does that on every call won't stay inside a 120 ms budget at 2,000 calls a second.

Lesson 1's store answered lookups with a hash map in RAM. That needs every key in memory, and it can't answer "every payment from 1,000 to 1,999". You want the keys in order, on disk.

Version 1 is a sorted array of `(key, row address)` pairs in a file. About 400 pairs fit in an 8 KB page, so a million keys take 2,500 pages, and a binary search over them reads about 12 pages, each at a different place in the file. That is tolerable. Inserting is not. A new key in the middle means shifting every pair after it, on average half the file: 1,250 pages rewritten for one insert.

Version 2 is a binary search tree on disk. Each node holds one key and two pointers, and an insert just adds a node. But a balanced tree of a million keys is 20 levels deep, so a lookup is 20 random page reads, and every 8 KB page holds a single 8-byte key.

Version 3 puts many keys in each node. Make a node one page: a sorted list of a few hundred keys, with a pointer to a child page next to each. Every step down now divides the search by a few hundred instead of by 2. With 400 children per node, one level covers 400 keys, two levels 160,000 and three levels 64 million. That is the **B-tree**, published by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight in 1970. Its variant, the B+tree, is the default index in PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL, and the format of SQLite's tables. The figure shows a toy one in which a node holds at most 3 keys. The rest of the lesson adds to this picture.

In the Try it, PostgreSQL's index on a million rows is 3 levels deep, and a lookup reads 4 pages: 3 index pages and the heap page that holds the row. The top two levels of that index are only 11 pages. Every lookup touches them, so their usage counts (lesson 3's tally of recent use) stay high, and the clock sweep keeps passing them by. A lookup on a busy server usually costs at most two reads from disk: the leaf and the heap page.

try.title: One row out of a million
steps: From `labs/`, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait` and open psql with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Create a million-row `payments` table with no index and look up one payment. Predict the `Buffers` line before you run it.
Add the primary key and run the same query twice. Predict how many pages it reads now.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
The table has 6,400 pages, and without an index the query reads all of them:

```text
 Seq Scan on payments (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Filter: (id = 424242)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 999999
   Buffers: shared hit=2304 read=4096
 ...
 Execution Time: 23.974 ms
```

With the primary key, the same query reads 4 pages, and the second run finds them all in shared_buffers:

```text
 Index Scan using payments_pkey on payments (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (id = 424242)
   Index Searches: 1
   Buffers: shared hit=4
 ...
 Execution Time: 0.031 ms
```

(output trimmed). Three of the 4 pages are the index's three levels and one is the heap page with the row. The whole index is 2,745 pages, and the lookup reads 3 of them. `ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY` builds the index by sorting all the keys and filling leaves from left to right, which is faster than a million inserts. Your timings differ.

sections.h: Internal nodes route the search, and leaves hold the data
sections.body:
There are two kinds of node in the figure.

A **leaf** is a node on the bottom level. It holds keys with their values, in key order. In a PostgreSQL index the value is the row's ctid, its (page, slot) address from lesson 2, so the leaf entry for payment 424242 says where that row lives. Each leaf also points to its right neighbour, so you can read every key in order by walking sideways along the bottom.

An **internal node** holds only **separator keys** and the page ids of its children. A node with n separators has n + 1 children, and the separators say which child covers which keys. The node `30 50` sends keys below 30 to its first child, 30 to 49 to its second, and 50 or more to its third. To find 60, start at the root: 60 is below 70, so go left. In `30 50`, 60 is at least 50, so take the third child. That leaf holds `50 60`. One page per level, three reads.

That is a B+tree. Bayer and McCreight's original B-tree also kept values in internal nodes, so some searches could stop halfway down. Moving every value into the leaves gives up that shortcut and buys two things. Internal nodes hold only keys and pointers, so more of them fit in a page: the tree gets wider, shorter, and small enough at the top to stay cached. And since every key is in a leaf and the leaves are linked, a range is one walk along the bottom level, as the last section shows.

The toy tree has **order 4**: a node has at most 4 children, so at most 3 keys. Books define "order" in different ways. This lesson and its lab use this one. A real page is far wider. A PostgreSQL index entry for an `int` key takes 20 bytes: an 8-byte entry header that holds the row's ctid, the key padded to 8 bytes, and a 4-byte line pointer (the slotted page of lesson 2 again). With a 24-byte page header and 16 bytes of B-tree data at the end of the page, (8,192 - 24 - 16) / 20 = 407 entries fit. The number of children per node is the **fanout**. With a fanout in the hundreds, an index stays at 3 or 4 levels for any table you will meet.

PostgreSQL adds two details you'll see in the Try it. Page 0 of every index is a metapage that says which page is the root. And every page except the rightmost one on its level starts with a **high key**, an upper bound for the keys allowed on that page, and keeps a link to its right sibling. PostgreSQL's B-tree follows Lehman and Yao's design from 1981, in which those two let a search that lands on a page another session has just split notice it and move right.

try.title: Read the pages of a real index
steps: In the same session, ask the metapage where the root is. `level` counts the levels below the root, so 0 means the root is a leaf.
List the root's first items. `ctid` holds the child's page number and `data` the separator key as little-endian bytes. Predict how many children the root has.
Look at leaf page 1, the leftmost leaf, then count pages and items per page type for the whole index (`l` leaf, `i` internal, `r` root).

code.title: psql

try.expect:
```text
 root | level
------+-------
  290 |     2

 itemoffset |  ctid   |          data
------------+---------+-------------------------
          1 | (3,0)   |
          2 | (289,1) | 09 96 01 00 00 00 00 00
          3 | (575,1) | 11 2c 03 00 00 00 00 00

 blkno | type | live_items | free_size | btpo_next
-------+------+------------+-----------+-----------
     1 | l    |        367 |       808 |         2

 itemoffset | ctid  |          data
------------+-------+-------------------------
          1 | (2,1) | 6f 01 00 00 00 00 00 00
          2 | (0,1) | 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
          3 | (0,2) | 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00

 type | pages | avg_items
------+-------+-----------
 i    |    10 |       274
 l    |  2733 |       367
 r    |     1 |        10
```

The root is page 290, and level 2 means two levels below it: 3 in all. In the root, the page number in `ctid` is the downlink. The first item has no key, so it covers everything below the second item's key: `09 96 01 00` read as a little-endian number is 104,969, so page 289 starts at payment 104,969. Leaf 1 holds 367 items and links to leaf 2. Its first item is the high key, 367 (`6f 01`), the first key of leaf 2. Then come the entries: key 1 points at heap row (0,1). 2,733 leaves of 367 keys hold the million rows. 367 is 90% of the 407 that would fit, because the index was built with the default fillfactor.

sections.h: A full node splits, and a root split grows the tree at the top
sections.body:
An insert starts as a search: walk down to the leaf where the key belongs and add it there, in order. Most of the time it fits, and the insert changes exactly one page.

Sometimes the leaf is full. Version 1 would make the page bigger, but a page has a fixed size, which is the whole point of pages. Version 2 would chain an overflow page to the full leaf. Every key that lands in that part of the index then piles into the chain, which must be read page by page: the slow linear search we were escaping.

Version 3 is the **split**, and the stepper walks through one. The full leaf gets a new right sibling, and the upper half of its keys moves there. The parent now needs a pointer to the new leaf and a separator saying where the new leaf starts. The separator is the new leaf's first key, and it is **copied** up: it stays in the leaf too, because the leaves must hold every key.

The parent may be full as well. Then it splits the same way, with one difference: its middle key is **pushed** up and leaves both halves, because keys in internal nodes are only signposts. Splits can climb all the way to the root. When the root splits, a new root with a single key is made above it. That is the only way a B+tree gets taller, so every leaf is always at the same depth.

A split leaves two half-full pages. With keys arriving in random order, pages refill unevenly, and the index settles at about two-thirds full: 64% to 67% for random UUIDs in our runs of the Try it. PostgreSQL treats one case specially. When the page that splits is the rightmost leaf, as it is when keys only grow (an identity column, or a time-ordered id), it keeps the left page 90% full, the B-tree default `fillfactor`. In one run of the Try it, 200,000 random UUIDs took 1,038 leaf pages, and 200,000 `uuidv7()` values, the time-ordered UUIDs PostgreSQL 18 added, took 767.

A split also costs writes. It changes the old leaf, the new leaf and the parent, and each of those changes goes through the write-ahead log of lesson 6.

try.title: Watch the first split
steps: Create a table with an `int` primary key and insert 407 rows. Predict the number of index pages and levels.
Insert row 408, then look at the metapage, every page, and the new root's items.

Fill one index with 200,000 time-ordered UUIDs and another with 200,000 random ones, then compare their leaf pages with `pgstatindex` (from the `pgstattuple` extension, which the image ships). Predict which one is bigger.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
407 keys fit in one leaf, which is also the root (page 1, level 0). Key 408 splits it:

```text
 root | level | pages
------+-------+-------
    1 |     0 |     2
...
 root | level | pages
------+-------+-------
    3 |     1 |     4

 blkno | type | live_items | btpo_prev | btpo_next
-------+------+------------+-----------+-----------
     1 | l    |        367 |         0 |         2
     2 | l    |         42 |         1 |         0
     3 | r    |          2 |         0 |         0

 itemoffset | ctid  |          data
------------+-------+-------------------------
          1 | (1,0) |
          2 | (2,1) | 6f 01 00 00 00 00 00 00
```

The tree grew a level at the top: a new root on page 3 points at leaf 1 and, from key 367 (`6f 01`) on, at leaf 2. This was the rightmost leaf, so PostgreSQL left it 90% full: 366 keys plus the high key 367. The other 42 keys moved right. Then the UUIDs:

```text
   t    | leaf_pages | avg_leaf_density
--------+------------+------------------
 ids_v7 |        767 |            89.91
 ids_v4 |       1038 |            66.52
```

Time-ordered keys always land in the rightmost leaf and leave pages 90% full. Random keys split pages in the middle and leave them two-thirds full, so the index needs about a third more pages for the same rows. The random numbers change from run to run: another run gave 1,083 pages at 63.77%.

sections.h: Range scans walk the leaves, and column order decides what an index can answer
sections.body:
`WHERE id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1999` is where the leaf chain pays off. The index descends once, to the leaf holding 1000: the same three page reads as a lookup. Then it reads keys along that leaf and follows the right-link to the next leaf, until it meets a key above 1999. A thousand keys at 367 per leaf span 3 or 4 leaves, so the scan reads 6 index pages in all. A thousand separate lookups would read 3,000.

An index on several columns sorts by the first column, then by the second within each value of the first, like a phone book sorted by last name and then first name. Take an index on `(region, batch_id)`. `WHERE region = 2 AND batch_id = 7700` is one descent to one spot. `WHERE batch_id = 7700` on its own is harder, because the matching entries sit in four places, one inside each region's run of entries. Before PostgreSQL 18 the choice was to read every leaf of the index or scan the table. PostgreSQL 18 added **skip scan**: it descends once per distinct region, as if you had written `region = 0`, then `region = 1`, and so on. In the Try it that costs 22 pages (`Index Searches: 6`) instead of 5,440 for a scan of the table. Skip scan only pays when the leading column has few distinct values. With 50,000 merchants in front, 50,000 descents lose to the table scan. Oracle has had index skip scans since version 9i.

The general rule, from the PostgreSQL docs: equality conditions on the leading columns, plus a range condition on the first column that has no equality, limit how much of the index is read. Put the equality columns first and the range column last.

Last question: what does a leaf point at? In PostgreSQL every index, the primary key included, stores ctids, and the row itself lives in the heap. That heap page is the fourth page in the first Try it. InnoDB, MySQL's engine, keeps the whole row in the leaves of the primary key index. That index is the table (a **clustered index**), and a secondary index stores the primary key, so a lookup through it descends two trees. Oracle offers both: ordinary tables are heaps like PostgreSQL's, and an index-organized table works like InnoDB's. Lesson 7 measures what each choice costs a query.

sections.h: A copy-on-write B-tree never overwrites a page
sections.body:
Every change in this lesson overwrites pages in place. An insert rewrites its leaf, and a split rewrites the leaf, its new sibling and the parent. If the power fails between those writes, the file holds half a split: a parent pointing at a page that was never written, or a new page that nothing points at. PostgreSQL, InnoDB and Oracle guard against that with a write-ahead log, which lesson 6 builds. There is a second answer: never overwrite a page that the current tree uses.

LMDB, the embedded key-value store written for OpenLDAP, works that way. To change a leaf, it writes a changed copy of the leaf to a free page. The parent must now point at the copy, so the parent is copied too, and so on up to a new root: one new page per level, three pages for a three-level tree, as the figure shows. Every page the change didn't touch is shared by the old tree and the new one. The commit is the last write: LMDB records the new root in one of two meta pages at the start of the file, taking turns between them. Until that write, the old root is the database. After a crash, LMDB opens the root that the newer meta page names, and its documentation says this design needs no special recovery procedure at all.

The old tree stays whole, so it is a free snapshot. A reader that started before the commit keeps walking root v1. Readers never wait for the writer, and the writer never waits for readers. LMDB frees an old version's pages once no reader uses that version, and keeps a list of free pages to reuse instead of growing the file.

The price is in writes and in concurrency. A one-row change copies a whole root-to-leaf path, where an in-place B+tree writes one leaf page plus a small log record. And LMDB lets only one write transaction run at a time. That suits read-heavy embedded use, such as a service's local cache or configuration store. A ledger taking thousands of concurrent writes wants the in-place tree and its log.

refs.title: LMDB: lmdb.h, the library's own description of its copy-on-write design

analogy: A B+tree works like the signs in a large warehouse. A board at the door says which aisles hold which range of item numbers, a sign at the head of each aisle says which shelf holds which range, and each shelf keeps its items in number order with a note pointing to the next shelf. Finding one item means reading the same three signs however big the warehouse is, and collecting items 1,000 to 1,999 means finding the first shelf and walking along. When a shelf overflows, a new shelf goes in next to it and the aisle sign gets one more line. The analogy breaks at growth: a warehouse grows by adding aisles at its edge, while a B+tree grows by putting a new sign above the door board, so every shelf stays the same number of signs from the entrance.
in_your_world: Every primary key and unique constraint in your payment schema is one of these trees, in Oracle and in PostgreSQL. The key type decides how it fills. A `bigint` from a sequence, or a `uuidv7()` id, always lands in the rightmost leaf, which PostgreSQL keeps 90% full. Random `gen_random_uuid()` idempotency keys land on a random leaf every time, leave pages two-thirds full and need that leaf in memory for every insert. On Oracle RAC the opposite problem shows up: every node inserting sequence values into the same rightmost block makes it hot, which is what Oracle's reverse key indexes exist for. For reads, a settlement query like `WHERE merchant_id = ? AND created_at >= ?` wants an index on `(merchant_id, created_at)` in that order: one descent, then a walk along the leaves.
mistake: The common mistake is putting the range column first in a composite index, for example `(created_at, merchant_id)` for queries that ask for one merchant's payments since a date. It feels natural to lead with time. But the index is sorted by `created_at` first, so the entries for merchant 42 are scattered among every other merchant's, and the scan reads every entry from that date on, then throws most of them away. People make it because both columns are "in the index" and EXPLAIN does show an index scan. The fix is to put equality columns first and the range column last, `(merchant_id, created_at)`, so the matching entries sit next to each other in the leaves. Compare `Buffers` in `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` for both orders.

compare.title: Where the row lives: PostgreSQL vs InnoDB

a.label: PostgreSQL
a.title: heap table + B-tree indexes
a.src:
primary key index (B+tree)
  leaf entry: (id 424242, ctid (2694,21))
             |
             v
heap: page 2694, slot 21 -> the row

secondary index on card
  leaf entry: ('card-4242', ctid (2694,21))

lookup by id:   3 index pages + 1 heap page
lookup by card: 3 index pages + 1 heap page

b.label: InnoDB (MySQL)
b.title: clustered primary key
b.src:
primary key index (B+tree) IS the table
  leaf entry: (id 424242, card, amount, ...)

secondary index on card
  leaf entry: ('card-4242', id 424242)
             |
             v
  then a second descent of the primary key

lookup by id:   3 pages, row included
lookup by card: 3 pages + 3 pages

compare.note: Both are B+trees; the difference is what a leaf holds. PostgreSQL's leaves hold physical addresses, so every index finds the row in one extra heap read, but an update that moves a row to another page must add entries to every index (lesson 2's HOT updates avoid that when they can). InnoDB's primary key leaves hold the row itself, so primary key lookups and ranges are cheaper, but every secondary lookup pays a second descent, and a wide or random primary key makes every secondary index bigger.

worked.title: Estimate how tall an index will be

steps.say: Start from the size of one leaf entry. For an `int` key in PostgreSQL: an 8-byte index tuple header (it holds the row's ctid), the 4-byte key padded to 8 bytes, and a 4-byte line pointer in the slot array.

Work out entries per page. The page loses 24 bytes to the page header and 16 to the B-tree's special space at the end, which holds the sibling links. Leaves built by CREATE INDEX, or filled by ascending inserts, are 90% full.
steps.code:
max per page  = (8192 - 24 - 16) / 20 = 407
per leaf (90%) = 407 x 0.9 = 366, plus the high key = 367

steps.say: Count the pages level by level, going up until one page is enough. That page is the root. Internal pages built by CREATE INDEX are fuller than half but not full; the Try it measured 274 downlinks each.
steps.code:
leaves   = 1,000,000 / 366 = 2,733
internal = 2,733 / 274    = 10
root     = 1  -> 3 levels: root, internal, leaf

steps.say: Check against the real index: `bt_metap` said level 2 (three levels) and `bt_multi_page_stats` counted 2,733 leaves and 10 internal pages. The same arithmetic in Kotlin shows how slowly height grows.

lab.title: Build a B+tree of order 4
steps: Open `BPlusTree.kt`. Read `Node`, `Leaf` and `Internal` at the top, then `childIndex` and `checkInvariants` at the bottom: the checker is the list of rules your tree must keep.
Run the tests once. All 10 fail.

Write `get`: start with `read(root)`, follow `children[childIndex(keys, key)]` while the node is `Internal`, then binary-search the leaf. Always follow pointers through `read`, which counts page reads.
Write `insert` for leaves (add in order, or replace an existing key) and `put`. Then write `splitLeaf` (copy the separator up) and the root case in `put` (a new `Internal` root, `height++`).
Write `splitInternal` (push the middle key up) and the internal branch of `insert`.
Write `range`: descend to the leaf where `lo` belongs, then walk keys and `next` links until a key is above `hi`. Run the tests until all 10 pass.
hints: `ArrayList.binarySearch` returns `-(insertionPoint + 1)` for a missing key, so `-(i + 1)` is where the new key goes.

A leaf split returns `Split(right.keys[0], rightId)` and keeps that key in the right leaf. An internal split returns `keys[mid]` and removes it from both halves: the left keeps `keys[0 until mid]` and `children[0..mid]`.
Before you link the new leaf, copy the old leaf's `next` into it: `right.next = leaf.next`, then `leaf.next = rightId`.
If "a range scan descends once" fails, you are probably descending again for each leaf, or reading the next leaf after you already found a key above `hi`.

drill.title: Write both splits from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. For a B+tree whose nodes hold `keys`, leaves hold `values` and `next`, and internal nodes hold `children`, write `splitLeaf` and `splitInternal`. Each returns the separator for the parent and the new node's page id. Then answer: which split keeps its separator in a child, and why?

answer.src:
fun splitLeaf(leaf: Leaf): Split {
    val mid = leaf.keys.size / 2
    val right = Leaf()
    right.keys += leaf.keys.subList(mid, leaf.keys.size)
    right.values += leaf.values.subList(mid, leaf.values.size)
    leaf.keys.subList(mid, leaf.keys.size).clear()
    leaf.values.subList(mid, leaf.values.size).clear()
    right.next = leaf.next                    // splice into the leaf chain
    val id = allocate(right)
    leaf.next = id
    return Split(right.keys[0], id)           // copy up: the key stays in the leaf
}

fun splitInternal(node: Internal): Split {
    val mid = node.keys.size / 2
    val up = node.keys[mid]
    val right = Internal()
    right.keys += node.keys.subList(mid + 1, node.keys.size)
    right.children += node.children.subList(mid + 1, node.children.size)
    node.keys.subList(mid, node.keys.size).clear()
    node.children.subList(mid + 1, node.children.size).clear()
    return Split(up, allocate(right))         // push up: the key leaves both halves
}

// The leaf split keeps its separator, because the leaves must hold every key and value.
// Internal keys are only signposts, so the middle one can move up.

recap: A B+tree index is a tree of pages. Each page holds hundreds of keys, so three or four levels cover any table, and a lookup reads one page per level.
Internal nodes hold separator keys and child page ids. Leaves hold every key with its value (a ctid in PostgreSQL) and link to the next leaf.
A full leaf splits and copies its new sibling's first key up. A full internal node splits and pushes its middle key up. A root split adds a level at the top, so every leaf stays at the same depth.
Random keys leave pages about two-thirds full. PostgreSQL keeps the rightmost leaf 90% full when it splits, so ascending keys such as `uuidv7()` make a denser index.
A range scan descends once and walks the leaf chain. A composite index serves equality on its leading columns plus one range; PostgreSQL 18's skip scan helps when the leading column has few values.

A copy-on-write B-tree such as LMDB's never overwrites a page in use: a change copies the path up to a new root, writing the new root into a meta page is the commit, old roots are free snapshots, and only one writer runs at a time.

quiz.q: A B+tree has about 400 children per internal node and 400 keys per leaf. Roughly how many levels does it need for 64 million keys?
quiz.why: 400 x 400 x 400 = 64 million: the root covers 400 internal nodes, each of which covers 400 leaves of 400 keys. 26 is log2 of 64 million, the height of a binary tree. Height grows with the logarithm to base 400, which is why real indexes stay at 3 or 4 levels.

quiz.q: In an order-4 B+tree (at most 3 keys per node), you insert 25 into the full leaf `10 20 30`. The leaf splits into `10 20` and `25 30`. What happens to 25?
options: It moves up to the parent and is removed from the leaf
Nothing goes up; the parent finds the new leaf through the leaf chain
It is copied up as the separator and stays as the first key of the right leaf
20 is copied up, because it is the last key of the left leaf
quiz.why: A leaf split copies the new leaf's first key into the parent and keeps it in the leaf, because the leaves must hold every key and its value. Moving the key up and out is what an internal split does with its middle key. The leaf chain is for range scans; searches only go down, so the parent needs the separator.

quiz.q: A settlement report runs `WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-11-01'`. Which index lets PostgreSQL read one contiguous run of leaf entries?
options: Either: both columns are in the index
Neither: a B-tree can't use two conditions at once
quiz.why: With `merchant_id` first, all of merchant 42's entries are together and sorted by time, so the scan starts at the first one on or after the date and stops at the next merchant. With `created_at` first, merchant 42's entries are scattered among every other merchant's since that date, and the scan reads and discards them. Equality columns first, range column last.

quiz.q: Two tables get 200,000 inserts each: one keyed by `uuidv7()`, the other by `gen_random_uuid()`. The random one's index has about a third more leaf pages. Why?
options: Random UUIDs are longer than time-ordered ones
Random keys split pages in the middle and leave them about two-thirds full, while ascending keys split the rightmost leaf, which PostgreSQL leaves 90% full
The random index has more levels, and each level adds pages
quiz.why: Both UUID types are 16 bytes. The difference is where inserts land: random keys hit pages all over the index, and each split leaves two half-full pages that refill unevenly, so leaves average about 66%. Time-ordered keys always go to the rightmost leaf, and PostgreSQL's rightmost split keeps the left page at the 90% fillfactor. Both indexes have the same number of levels.

quiz.q: From lesson 3: a primary key lookup reads the root, an internal page, a leaf and a heap page. On a busy server with a big table, which of these is most likely to need a read from disk?
options: The root, because it is the first page read
All four equally, because the clock sweep treats every page the same
The leaf and the heap page
None: index pages are never evicted
quiz.why: Every lookup pins the root and one of a few internal pages, so their usage counts stay at or near 5 and the clock sweep keeps passing them by. There are thousands of leaves and heap pages, and each one is touched rarely, so those are the pages that drop to usage 0 and get evicted. Index pages have no special protection; they stay because they are used.

flashcards.front: How does a copy-on-write B-tree such as LMDB commit a change?
flashcards.back: It writes changed copies of the leaf and of every page above it up to a new root, then records the new root in a meta page. The old root stays whole as a snapshot.

flashcards.front: Leaf split vs internal split: what happens to the separator?
flashcards.back: A leaf split copies the new leaf's first key up and keeps it in the leaf. An internal split pushes its middle key up and removes it from both halves.

flashcards.front: Why is every leaf of a B+tree at the same depth?
flashcards.back: The tree only grows when the root splits and a new root is added above it. It grows at the top, never at the bottom.

flashcards.front: Why do databases use B+trees rather than the original B-tree?
flashcards.back: Internal nodes hold only keys and pointers, so fanout is higher and the tree is shorter, and linked leaves make range scans a walk along the bottom level.

flashcards.front: How many `int` index entries fit in a PostgreSQL B-tree page, and how full are leaves after CREATE INDEX?
flashcards.back: 407 entries of 20 bytes. Leaves are filled to the default fillfactor of 90%, about 367 entries.

flashcards.front: What does a PostgreSQL B-tree high key do?
flashcards.back: It is the first item on every page except the rightmost on its level: an upper bound for the page's keys. With the right-link it lets a search that hits a just-split page move right (Lehman and Yao).

flashcards.front: What does PostgreSQL 18's B-tree skip scan do?
flashcards.back: For a condition on a later column of a multicolumn index, it descends once per distinct value of the leading column. It pays off only when that column has few distinct values.

terms.plain: A balanced tree of pages whose internal nodes hold only separator keys and whose linked leaves hold every key and value.
How many children an internal node has. Hundreds per 8 KB page in a real index.
A key in an internal node that says which child covers which range of keys.
Moving half of a full node's keys to a new sibling and adding a separator for it to the parent.
A B-tree that never overwrites a page in use: a change writes new copies up to a new root, and switching to that root is the commit.
How full PostgreSQL packs B-tree leaves when it builds an index or splits the rightmost leaf. 90% by default.
An index whose leaves hold the table's rows themselves, as InnoDB's primary key does.
Using a multicolumn index without a condition on its first column, by searching once per distinct value of that column.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why a primary key lookup on a 1-million-row table reads 4 pages, and whether it will read 40 when the table has 100 million rows. Explain how the index is built and what happens to the cost as the table grows.
explain_back.answer: The index is a B+tree whose nodes are 8 KB pages holding a few hundred keys each. Internal pages hold separator keys and pointers to child pages; leaves hold every key with the row's address. A lookup starts at the root and reads one page per level until it reaches the leaf, then reads the heap page with the row. At a million rows the index has three levels: a root, about ten internal pages and about 2,700 leaves, so the lookup reads three index pages plus one heap page. Each extra level multiplies capacity by the fanout, a few hundred, so 100 million rows need only one more level: about 5 page reads, not 40. And the root and internal pages are touched by every lookup, so they stay in memory and only the leaf and heap page usually come from disk.

deeper.body:
**Many sessions in one tree.** A real index is read and changed by many backends at once. The textbook method is latch crabbing: hold a short lock (a latch) on a node, take the child's latch, and release the parent's once the child is safe, meaning it can't split. Inserts that might split hold latches on the whole path that could split. PostgreSQL instead follows Lehman and Yao (1981): a reader holds only one page lock at a time, and if a concurrent split moved its key to the right sibling, the page's high key tells it so and it follows the right-link. The nbtree README covers how a split is logged as one WAL record for the split pages and a second for the parent, with a flag on the left page until the parent has its downlink.

**Pages that never merge.** Textbooks merge or rebalance nodes that fall below half full after deletes. PostgreSQL's README says merging partly full pages "seems impractical": it only deletes a page once it is completely empty. So an index that lost most of its rows stays big until `REINDEX`, or `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` on a live system.

**Duplicates and dead entries.** Since PostgreSQL 13, a leaf stores many equal keys as one key with a posting list of ctids (deduplication, on by default), which shrinks indexes on columns like `status`. Since PostgreSQL 14, bottom-up index deletion removes entries pointing at dead row versions just before a page would split, so a table with many updates splits less.

**Building bottom-up.** `CREATE INDEX` on a full table doesn't insert row by row. It sorts all the keys, writes leaves left to right at the fillfactor, then builds each level above from the first key of each page below. That is why a freshly built index is dense and fast to create.
